lead: The F-test for equality of variances compares two sample variances. If two independent samples come from normal populations with the same variance, the ratio F = s1²/s2² follows an F distribution. A ratio far from 1 is evidence that the population variances differ. Engineers use it to compare fill-volume spread from two machines, variability of two suppliers, or measurement error from two instruments. This chapter gives the test procedure, the degrees of freedom, and the table reading. It links the F ratio to the ANOVA idea in Chapter 6.6.
prereq: You need Unit 5 (the F distribution), Unit 3 (the normal distribution), and Chapter 6.1 for null hypotheses, p-values and decisions.

blocks.text: The test starts with two independent random samples. Sample 1 has size n1 and sample variance s1². Sample 2 has size n2 and sample variance s2². Each sample variance estimates its population variance, σ1² and σ2². If the populations are normal and σ1² = σ2², the ratio of the sample variances has a known distribution. That distribution is the F distribution from Unit 5.
F = s1² / s2²,  df1 = n1 − 1,  df2 = n2 − 1
blocks.where: s1² and s2² are the sample variances; n1 and n2 are the sample sizes; df1 is the numerator degrees of freedom and df2 is the denominator degrees of freedom.

blocks.text: Why a ratio? A single sample variance can be large or small by chance. The ratio cancels the common population variance. Under H0: σ1² = σ2², F should be near 1. Values far above 1 suggest σ1² > σ2². Values far below 1 suggest σ1² < σ2². The F distribution is skewed right and takes only positive values. Its shape depends on both df1 and df2.

The assumptions are independent random samples and normal populations. The test is sensitive to non-normality: a heavy-tailed population can produce false alarms. Some syllabi call it the variance ratio test.

Fix the alternative before looking at the data. A one-tailed test asks whether one variance is larger. A two-tailed test asks whether the variances differ in either direction. For a one-tailed test with H1: σ1² > σ2², put sample 1 on top. If the data give s2² > s1², the test cannot reject in that direction; you can still compute F = s1²/s2² and get a value below 1.

items: State H0: σ1² = σ2² and H1: σ1² > σ2², or σ1² < σ2², or σ1² ≠ σ2².
Compute s1² and s2² with divisor n − 1 for each sample.
For H1: σ1² > σ2², set F = s1²/s2² with df1 = n1 − 1 and df2 = n2 − 1. For H1: σ1² < σ2², swap the labels or use F = s2²/s1².
For H1: σ1² ≠ σ2², put the larger sample variance in the numerator. Then F ≥ 1, df1 belongs to that sample, and df2 belongs to the other sample. Compare with F(α/2, df1, df2).
Reject H0 if F is greater than the critical value. Otherwise fail to reject H0.

blocks.text: For the one-tailed upper test, the critical value is F(α, df1, df2). For the two-tailed test, use α/2 because both tails matter. Tables usually give upper-tail values. That is why the larger variance goes on top in the two-tailed case; the lower tail is handled by the test structure, not by a negative F. With software, use the p-value. Reject when p ≤ α.

F tables are indexed by df1 across the top and df2 down the side. The order matters: F(0.05, 9, 11) is not F(0.05, 11, 9). Always write the df pair in the order (numerator, denominator). Report the sample sizes, sample variances, F statistic, df pair, critical value or p-value, and decision. A conclusion in words: “At the 5% level, the evidence shows that Machine 1 has a larger variance than Machine 2.” Do not say “accept H0”; say “fail to reject H0”. The F-test does not tell you which mean is larger. It only compares spread. Use it before a two-sample t-test when the equal-variance assumption matters; see Chapter 6.3. For more than two groups, the same F ratio appears in ANOVA; see Chapter 6.6.

figure.caption: Sample variances 16 and 4 form F = 4.00 with df (9, 11). The critical value 2.90 is crossed, so the null hypothesis is rejected.

spec.title: Variance ratio test
spec.aria: A flowchart takes two sample variances into an F ratio of 4.00, compares it with a critical value of 2.90, and rejects the null hypothesis.

examples.question: Two machines fill bottles. Machine 1: n1 = 10, s1 = 4.0 ml. Machine 2: n2 = 12, s2 = 2.0 ml. Test H0: σ1² = σ2² against H1: σ1² > σ2² at α = 0.05. Use F(0.05, 9, 11) = 2.90.
steps: Machine 1 variance: s1² = 4.0² = 16.0 ml². Machine 2 variance: s2² = 2.0² = 4.0 ml².
Degrees of freedom: df1 = n1 − 1 = 10 − 1 = 9. df2 = n2 − 1 = 12 − 1 = 11.
The alternative is σ1² > σ2², so sample 1 stays in the numerator. F = s1²/s2² = 16.0/4.0 = 4.00.
Critical value from the F table: F(0.05, 9, 11) = 2.90.
Compare: 4.00 > 2.90. Reject H0 at the 5% level.
Conclusion: the evidence shows that Machine 1 has a larger fill-volume variance than Machine 2.
examples.answer: At the 5% level, reject H0: the evidence shows that Machine 1 has a larger fill-volume variance than Machine 2.
examples.check:
s1 = 4.0
s2 = 2.0
n1 = 10
n2 = 12
F = s1**2 / s2**2
df1 = n1 - 1
df2 = n2 - 1
crit = 2.90
print(F)
print(df1)
print(df2)
print(crit)
print(int(F > crit))

traps: For a two-tailed test use α/2 in the F table. Using α gives a critical value that is too small and rejects H0 too often.
Check the df order: F(0.05, 9, 11) is not F(0.05, 11, 9). The first df is the numerator variance's df.
For H1: σ1² > σ2², keep sample 1 in the numerator. Do not automatically put the larger variance on top unless you also swap the hypotheses and df.
The F-test assumes normal populations. A skewed sample can give a small p-value from skew, not from unequal variances.
Sample variances use divisor n − 1. Using n gives a biased ratio and wrong df.

quiz.q: State the F statistic for comparing two variances and its two degrees of freedom.
quiz.a: F = s1²/s2², where s1² and s2² are sample variances. df1 = n1 − 1 and df2 = n2 − 1.

quiz.q: Why does the two-tailed F-test put the larger sample variance in the numerator?
quiz.a: F tables usually give upper-tail values. Putting the larger variance on top gives F ≥ 1, so one upper-tail comparison with α/2 handles the two-sided test without a lower-tail table.

quiz.q: Sample A: n = 8, s² = 25. Sample B: n = 10, s² = 9. Test H0: σA² = σB² against H1: σA² > σB² at α = 0.05. Use F(0.05, 7, 9) = 3.29.
quiz.a: dfA = 7, dfB = 9. F = 25/9 = 2.78. Critical value = 3.29. Since 2.78 < 3.29, fail to reject H0. There is no significant evidence that σA² is larger.

quiz.q: A researcher applies the F-test to strongly skewed data and gets p = 0.01. Why is the conclusion uncertain?
quiz.a: The F-test assumes normal populations. Skewness can make the F ratio and its p-value unreliable, so the small p-value may come from non-normality. A robust spread test or a transformation is safer.

quiz.q: List the two main assumptions of the F-test for equality of variances.
quiz.a: Independent random samples, and normal populations.

quiz.q: For H1: σ1² ≠ σ2² with α = 0.05, which upper-tail level is read from the F table?
quiz.a: α/2 = 0.025, because the two-tailed test splits 5% into two tails of 2.5% each.

quiz.q: An F-test gives F = 0.4 with df (6, 10) for H1: σ1² > σ2². At α = 0.05, F critical = 3.22. What is the decision?
quiz.a: F = 0.4 is below 1 and far below 3.22, so fail to reject H0. The upper-tail test has no evidence that σ1² > σ2².

beyond: Not for the exam. Real data are rarely perfectly normal, so engineers often use Levene's test or the Brown–Forsythe test, which compare spread without the normal assumption. Bartlett's test is a likelihood-based variance test that still assumes normality. In industry, variance ratio ideas appear in quality control, supplier comparison and A/B testing of variability. Search next for Levene's test, robust tests for equality of variances, and the F distribution degrees of freedom.
